data.text/markdown:
⛰️ Rolling downhill

Structure optimization with ASE and the UMA machine-learning potential

Every arrangement of atoms has an energy. Nature prefers low energy, so molecules and crystals settle into shapes where nudging any atom in any direction would only raise the energy. Finding that shape on a computer is called structure optimization (or geometry relaxation), and it is the first step of almost every computational chemistry and materials science workflow. The idea fits in one sentence: follow the forces until they vanish. The force on each atom points downhill on the energy landscape, so we move the atoms along the forces, recompute, and repeat until every force is tiny. In this notebook you will:
  1. Be the optimizer by stepping a two-atom molecule downhill by hand.
  2. Relax a real molecule that we deliberately scramble, and watch it find its way home.
  3. Race the optimizers that ship with ASE against each other.
  4. Relax a crystal, including the size of its unit cell, and read off its lattice constant and stiffness.
Everything is live: change a control and the cells that depend on it re-run automatically.
▶️ Only seeing text, no sliders or plots? The notebook hasn't been run yet. Switch to the editor view and click Run all (or set Settings → Runtime → On startup to autorun), then switch back to app view. The first run installs the packages and downloads the UMA model, so give it a minute or two. You also need a (free) Hugging Face token with access to UMA: see section 0.
🧰 The tools we're using
  • ASE (the Atomic Simulation Environment) is a Python library for building, manipulating, and simulating atomic structures. It provides the Atoms object, the optimizers, and a common calculator interface for computing energies and forces.
  • UMA (Universal Model for Atoms, from Meta's FAIR Chemistry team) is a universal machine-learning interatomic potential. It was trained on hundreds of millions of quantum-mechanical (DFT) calculations spanning molecules, materials, catalysts, and more, and it reproduces DFT energies and forces across most of the periodic table while running thousands of times faster. That speed is what makes this notebook interactive. We use the small model, UMA-S 1.2.1 (uma-s-1p2p1).

0 · Load the potential

First we create an ASE calculator: the object that, given atom positions, returns the energy and forces. With UMA it takes two lines: load the model once (a predictor), then wrap it in a calculator for the kind of system you are simulating. 
import torch
from fairchem.core import FAIRChemCalculator, pretrained_mlip

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"   # use the GPU if there is one
predictor = pretrained_mlip.get_predict_unit("uma-s-1p2p1", device=device)
calc = FAIRChemCalculator(predictor, task_name="omol")    # molecules
UMA is one network with several task heads, one per family of training data, each matching a different DFT setup. We use two of them:
task_name Trained on Used here for
"omol" molecules (ωB97M-V hybrid DFT) sections 1–3. Needs the total charge and spin multiplicity spin in atoms.info (default: neutral singlet).
"omat" inorganic crystals (PBE / PBE+U) section 4
The notebook picks the right head automatically: periodic systems get omat, isolated molecules get omol.

data.text/markdown:
1 · Be the optimizer 🧑‍🔬

The simplest possible "structure" is two atoms joined by a bond. Its energy depends on just one number, the bond length ||(r||), so the energy landscape is a curve you can see. The force is the negative slope of that curve, ||(F = -\,\mathrm{d}E/\mathrm{d}r||). A positive force pushes the atoms apart (bond too short); a negative force pulls them together (bond too long). Steepest descent, the most basic optimizer, moves along the force with a fixed step size ||(\alpha||): ||[ r_{\text{new}} = r_{\text{old}} + \alpha\, F(r_{\text{old}}) ||]Your turn. Pick a molecule and a starting bond length, then press Take a step and watch the ball roll. Then try a bigger ||(\alpha||) and see what goes wrong.

Near the minimum the curve looks like a parabola, ||(E \approx \tfrac12 k (r-r_\mathrm{min})^2||), with stiffness ||(k \approx 5||) eV/Å². One steepest-descent step multiplies the distance from the minimum by ||((1-\alpha k)||). If ||(\alpha > 2/k \approx 0.3906||) Å²/eV, that factor is bigger than 1 in size and every step lands further away. Stiff bonds (N₂, CO) need smaller steps than soft ones (H₂, Cl₂). Real optimizers avoid this trap by learning the curvature as they go.

data.text/markdown:
2 · Relax a real molecule 🧪

With ||(N||) atoms the energy depends on ||(3N||) coordinates at once, so we can no longer draw the landscape. The recipe is unchanged, though, and ASE packages it into a few lines: 
from ase.build import molecule
from ase.optimize import BFGS

atoms = molecule("H2O")                # 1. build a structure
atoms.rattle(stdev=0.2)                # 2. (here) scramble it on purpose
atoms.calc = FAIRChemCalculator(predictor, task_name="omol")  # 3. attach UMA (molecule head)
BFGS(atoms).run(fmax=0.02)             # 4. step until every force < 0.02 eV/Å
fmax is the convergence criterion: the run stops once the largest force on any atom drops below it. Below, we shake a molecule with random displacements and let an optimizer bring it back. Drag the step slider under the plots to replay the trajectory, and hover over atoms to see their forces.

The reference column is the tabulated G2 geometry shipped with ASE. The relaxed bonds won't match it perfectly: the reference (MP2) and UMA's omol head (ωB97M-V) use different levels of theory, so differences of ~0.01 Å are expected.
A strong shake can knock the molecule over a hill into a different valley: a different conformer (e.g. a rotated OH group in ethanol) or even broken bonds. A local optimizer only ever goes downhill, so it finds the nearest minimum, not necessarily the lowest one. Finding the global minimum needs different tools (conformer searches, basin hopping, …).

data.text/markdown:
3 · The optimizer race 🏁

Steepest descent is simple but slow. ASE ships smarter algorithms that differ in how they decide where to step next:
Optimizer Idea in one line
BFGS Builds up an estimate of the landscape's curvature (the Hessian) and jumps toward the bottom of the local bowl. The usual default.
LBFGS Same idea, but remembers only the last few steps. Uses far less memory for big systems.
FIRE Rolls like a ball with friction (molecular dynamics), stopping whenever it starts going uphill. Very robust.
MDMin Also dynamics-based: moves atoms like a ball and kills the velocity when it points uphill.
GPMin Fits a Gaussian-process surrogate to the energies seen so far and minimizes that. Few steps, but each one costs more.
All five start from the same shaken molecule you set up above, so change the molecule or the shake and the race re-runs.

data.text/markdown:
4 · Relax a crystal 💎

In a crystal the atoms repeat forever in a unit cell. Besides the atom positions, the shape and size of the cell can also be wrong. The cell feels a "force" too: the stress (pressure). A squeezed crystal pushes outward; a stretched one pulls inward. ASE lets an optimizer move the cell by wrapping the atoms in a filter that bundles the stress together with the atomic forces: 
from ase.build import bulk
from ase.filters import FrechetCellFilter

atoms = bulk("Cu", "fcc", a=3.80, cubic=True)   # deliberately strained
atoms.calc = FAIRChemCalculator(predictor, task_name="omat")   # crystal head
BFGS(FrechetCellFilter(atoms)).run(fmax=0.01)   # relax positions AND cell
print(atoms.cell.cellpar())                     # relaxed lattice constant
Pick a crystal and strain it. Then compare relaxing atoms only with atoms + cell.

data.text/markdown:
🧭 Recap

  • An optimizer follows the forces downhill until the largest force falls below fmax.
  • The step size matters: steepest descent with too large a step overshoots and diverges. Smarter optimizers (BFGS, FIRE, …) adapt automatically.
  • Local optimizers find the nearest minimum, which isn't always the global one.
  • For crystals, the cell must be relaxed too, using a filter like FrechetCellFilter. Symmetry alone can make atomic forces vanish in a badly strained crystal.
  • A universal ML potential like UMA makes all of this fast enough to explore interactively. Pick the task head that matches your system (omol for molecules, omat for inorganic crystals). For publication-quality numbers, it's common to refine the final structure with DFT.

🧪 Things to try

  1. Set the shake strength to 0.4 Å on ethanol and check the bond table: did a bond break or the molecule change conformer?
  2. In the race, tighten fmax to 0.005 and see which optimizer struggles most near the end.
  3. Relax all six crystals in section 4 and compare with experiment. The omat head learned PBE, which tends to overestimate lattice constants by about 1%. Does UMA follow that trend?
  4. Compress NaCl by −8% and watch how hard it pushes back compared with tungsten.

📋 Cheat sheet

from ase.build import molecule, bulk
from ase.optimize import BFGS
from ase.filters import FrechetCellFilter
from ase.io import write
from fairchem.core import FAIRChemCalculator, pretrained_mlip
import torch

# needs a Hugging Face token with UMA access: set HF_TOKEN or run `hf auth login`
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
predictor = pretrained_mlip.get_predict_unit("uma-s-1p2p1", device=device)

# Molecule: relax atomic positions
mol = molecule("CH3CH2OH")
mol.info.update(charge=0, spin=1)          # neutral singlet
mol.calc = FAIRChemCalculator(predictor, task_name="omol")
BFGS(mol, trajectory="ethanol.traj").run(fmax=0.02)   # view with: ase gui ethanol.traj

# Crystal: relax positions + cell
si = bulk("Si", "diamond", a=5.6, cubic=True)
si.calc = FAIRChemCalculator(predictor, task_name="omat")
BFGS(FrechetCellFilter(si)).run(fmax=0.01)
print(si.cell.cellpar())
write("si_relaxed.cif", si)
